lignes.texte: 3 seconds… that’s all it takes to lose control of your life.
Your phone rings, you pick it up and say “Hello.” Nothing comes back but total silence. You hang
up and forget about it. But two weeks later, your family gets a frantic call.
It’s your voice, begging for help. Except… you're sitting right next to them.
An invisible attacker weaponized your identity, and you gave them everything
they needed with just one word. As technology has advanced,
so too have the tools at a scammer’s disposal. No one was on the other end of the phone during
those 3 seconds of dead air. You were talking to a predator. An automated machine known as a
predictive dialer. For places like legitimate businesses like call centers, the technology
has become a game-changer. Instead of humans manually typing in numbers, predictive dialers
can call multiple numbers at the same time. It analyzes the availability of staff, perfectly
calculating when someone is free to talk. But in the murky world of scammers,
this efficiently can reach terrifying heights. Old school cold calling was like a single
fisherman with a rod trying to catch one fish at a time. But today, it’s a giant net trawling an
ocean of phone numbers. It never sleeps and never complains and never feels guilty. If
no one picks up, it moves on. If a call goes to an answering machine, it’s a non-starter.
But if you pick up when the machine calls… it hauls you in.
You've just become a confirmed live number. That data alone can be worth a fortune. Databases
of verified numbers can be packaged, bundled and sold on the Dark Web to the highest bidder.
Just that one word, your simple hello, provided the AI system with a trove of valuable,
potentially exploitable, information. The AI detected what language you spoke.
A scammer's target may be English speakers, or Spanish speakers,
or Chinese speakers. The AI has already listed you as an active number and English speaker.
The software can also analyze how you speak. Do you have a strong regional accent? Does
your pronunciation or vocabulary suggest a particular educational background? The
Wall Street Journal in 2026 asked, “Has Your Accent Just Become a Security Vulnerability?”
If someone is going to scam you, sounding familiar can sometimes help establish trust. In
the case of strong regional accents, a scammer might make assumptions, rightly or wrongly,
about your background and how you will respond when asked a certain question.
Research shows that different economic brackets are often susceptible to differing psychological
triggers. People in low-incomes tend to fall more for fake job offers,
debt relief and fake lottery scams. But people with disposable capital, often over-confident
about their tech saviness, often fall for scams which promise to grow their wealth quickly.
All of this can be useful for a scamming operation.
Modern AI systems can also estimate your age from the sound of your voice. These systems
analyze hundreds of acoustic characteristics, including pitch, rhythm, speaking speed and
subtle variations that the human ear might miss. The systems are usually accurate at getting your
age within 5 years. This also matters.
The FBI has warned that criminal call centers deliberately target older people, sometimes with
very devastating consequences. When elderly people believe they’re speaking with trusted authorities,
charities or financial advisers, they tend to be more trusting than people who’ve grown up
in a world of digital skepticism. Romance scammers often target
elderly women. These are often educated, computer-literate women, but the criminals
are skilled at exploiting emotional vulnerability. In Britain, figures released by Action Fraud in
2019 showed that 63% of reported romance-fraud victims in 2018 were women. Victims lost an
average of £11,100, almost $15,000 at the time. The average victim was 50 years old, and women
lost twice as much money as men on average. Things are different in some parts of Asia
where it’s often young women who are the target. In South Korea, a study published in 2023 analyzed
280 romance-scam reports made to police during the first 6 months of 2022. It found that 71.4%
of victims were female. Unlike the older victims often highlighted in Western reports,
52.1% of these South Korean victims were in their 20s or younger, while
another 35.4% were in their thirties. Scammers don't always want the same
kind of victim. Different scams exploit different circumstances.
That’s why an automated AI system analyzing that one “Hello” is so important.
In 3 seconds of silence, the AI system has now figured out language, sex, earnings,
and age. That profile becomes part of a package bought by someone who intends to defraud people.
Because these automated calling systems call multiple times until someone picks up,
the scammers will also have information as to the time of day their mark is free to speak.
So next to estimated age, wage, sex, language, dialect, the package
now also includes the best time to reach you. And these scams aren’t always looking to empty
your bank account. Scammers often look for people who are prepared to send them small donations,
maybe for a local charity or maybe even for a political cause. If you fell for it, you might
have unknowingly been placed on a list: The Sucker List.
Your number has been associated with someone who is likely to fall for a scam. Your details are now
part of a large industry of scamming networks. The BBC said British researchers discovered at
least 160,000 people from England, Scotland and Wales on the Sucker List. These people
were sold as profiles, sometimes quite detailed. A researcher said, “You can buy details as specific
as people who are 80, disabled, live alone, respond to communication and play the Lottery.”
Why does the Lottery matter? Because the person might
be desperate and take chances. Someone in 2024 wrote on Quora:
“Why am I suddenly getting about 10 calls a day on my cell phone where I answer,
no one is there, and the call disconnects after 5 seconds?”
It’s possible his number had been sold on the Dark Web to scammers alongside thousands of millions of
other numbers. The scammers calling him daily might have been making sure it was active.
But they might have been doing much more than building a profile.
Every time this person said Hello into a machine or asked who was on the line,
those words were potentially raw material for an AI voice-cloning attack.
Voice cloning has become another weapon in what is known as vishing, or voice phishing.
The most unnerving recent example of this was in 2025 when scammers used AI to imitate the
voice of Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto. The criminals contacted a number of well-known
business leaders in Italy, pretending to represent Crosetto and his ministry. They claimed that
Italian journalists had been kidnapped in the Middle East and that ransom money was
urgently needed to secure their release. The scammers said the government couldn't
pay the money directly, but these wealthy business leaders could help their country
by providing the funds. They were assured that the Bank of Italy would reimburse them.
One of the targets was Massimo Moratti, the former owner of Inter Milan football club.
He fell for it. But Moratti wasn’t stupid. The person on the other
end of the line sounded exactly like Crosetto. Moratti made two transfers totaling approximately
one million euros, or about $1.1 million. Fortunately, Italian investigators managed
to trace and freeze nearly the entire sum in a Dutch bank account.
That’s the one thing scammers can’t fake: the place where the money is sent.
But the damage demonstrated something very disturbing about modern life.
Criminals had impersonated one of Italy's most senior government officials and convinced an
experienced businessman to transfer a fortune. Vishing scams are already a major global problem.
At the time the Crosetto case appeared in the Italian media, other reports emerged about an
elderly Italian lady who believed she’d received a call from her daughter asking
for money. The daughter was hysterical. Her husband had apparently had a car accident
that had injured a mother and her child. The elderly lady took pity on her daughter
and transferred €30,000, or $33,000. Vishing is not always about money.
In 2026, an attack embarrassed the telecommunications and mass media company, Charter
Communications. Using a voice clone, the scammers pretended to be staff and were given access to 4.9
million records. It was a score that could be sold on the Dark Web or used by the scammers.
You could be next because the fact is, almost anyone – provided they have a
moral deficit – can join the voice scamming game. With modern voice-cloning software now so widely
available, criminals no longer need hours of recordings to create a convincing imitation.
Tests carried out by cybersecurity company McAfee in 2023, just 3 seconds of recorded speech was
enough to produce a clone with an 85% voice match. With additional recordings and effort,
its researchers achieved a 95% match. No one would be able to tell the difference
between 95% real and the real thing. And almost anyone can access the
software because it's become so cheap. Some voice-cloning tools are available for free,
while others cost just a few dollars a month. In other words, what once required specialist
technology and considerable expertise to use is now available to anyone
who’s motivated to get into the scamming game. But surely these companies selling the software
build safeguards into their products? The answer is no.
Consumer Reports investigated 6 companies selling voice-cloning software in March 2025. They found
that 4 lacked meaningful technical safeguards to prevent someone from cloning another person's
voice without permission. Those 4 had no technical mechanisms to verify that the person whose voice
was being cloned had actually consented. All the user had to do was tick a box
claiming they had permission, or make a similar declaration. In most cases,
opening an account required little more than a name or email address – not even a reliable ID.
It’s like selling digital lockpicks to the general public and asking customers to promise
they won't break into anyone's house. Once scammers have your voice cloned,
they can use free generative AI systems such as ChatGPT or Claude to collect publicly available
information about you and build a personality profile. Personal information can be bought on
the Dark Web, but a surprising amount can also be found online. Depending on how much you've
shared publicly, someone might be able to discover where you live, what job you do,
who you're married to, and who your siblings and friends are… all by searching the internet.
And if they examine enough comments on your public social media profiles, they can feed your words
into an AI system to analyze your vocabulary, expressions and writing style. Combined with
a cloned voice, that information could help a scammer create an imitation of you that doesn't
just sound like you, but also speaks in a way that seems familiar to the people who know you.
In less than a few hours, they can talk like you, sound like you, and pretty much, be you.
An article in the Guardian in 2024 cited research by Starling Bank that revealed that 28% of people
had been targeted by an AI voice cloning scam at least once in the year. The research also showed
that 46% of respondents had no idea voice-clone scams existed. 8% said they’d hand over cash if
their loved one asked for some over the phone even if they thought something seemed a little off.
For scammers, the beauty of phone scams is that you can be a little
off and still get away with it. Grammar doesn't have to be perfect in
speech. Phone audio is compressed. There's often background noise, static, or poor reception. As
long as the AI gets the pitch, tone, rhythm and pronunciation reasonably close, the synthetic
voice might be convincing enough to fool someone, especially during a brief, emotional conversation.
The new software isn’t text-to-speech but it’s able to do real-time voice conversions. Instead
of typing words and waiting for the computer to speak them, a scammer can talk directly into a
microphone. AI software processes their speech almost instantaneously, transforming it into a
synthetic imitation of somebody else's voice. The scammer can now have a two-way
conversation. They can answer questions, interrupt, express fear or urgency,
and improvise as the conversation develops. And the scammer doesn't even have to sound
remotely like that person in real life. A high-pitched male with a
strong Scottish accent can easily become a woman from the deep south of the US.
It’s not ideal, but if the scammer didn’t want to talk at all,
he could allow the AI to respond itself. Of course, for the scammer, there’s a major
problem: The number they’re using might not match the number of the voice-cloned caller.
This is a real setback, but the person could say they’ve lost their phone,
or they’re using their friend’s phone. But this could never happen to you, right? You’d
know. You’re too smart to be fooled like that. Well, the human mind is very good at recognizing
voices. When someone sounds exactly like a person we know, it doesn’t compute that this person might
not actually be them. Neuroscience tells us that familiar voices are processed by brain networks
that interpret memories of bonding and experience. That’s why the very sound of someone’s voice can
sometimes bring relief, or maybe dread. A voice is a powerful thing.
And that's exactly what voice-cloning scammers are exploiting.
In a corporate situation, the scammer has another psychological weapon: authority.
Decades of research into obedience and social influence have shown that people can be overly
willing to follow instructions from someone they regard as an authority figure, even when
those instructions make them very uncomfortable. The Milgram obedience experiment in the 1960s
provided a shocking example: Subordinates are usually willing to do almost anything - in this
Milgram case, give people electric shocks - when told to by an authority figure.
In the workplace with today’s vishing scams, a subordinate might be reluctant to question an
urgent demand from a superior, especially when the consequences of refusing could be serious.
The scammers understand this. They purposefully use the language of a superior speaking to a
subordinate. They create urgency. They imply that questioning the request could get them in trouble.
And as we saw with the Charter Communications scam, it can work at the highest levels.
That’s another reason why Vishing is the new normal in the world of scamming.
In 2026, the FBI for the first time in 25 years in its Internet Crime Report had an
entire section devoted solely to AI-related scams. These scams accounted for $893.3 million of losses
across nearly 22,400 complaints. The vast majority were investment scams. They accounted for around
4,400 incidents and $632 million in losses. Extortion was next at just under 1,800 scams.
But the report noted that it was especially prevalent in “distress” scams -- when a family
member is informed about a problem that will require money to help someone. Sometimes it’s
money for bail. Sometimes medical fees. Sometimes it’s a ransom for a kidnapped family member.
Altogether, these vishing scams in the US cost Americans about $5 million in 2025.
Every week, someone new falls for it. And the cases have been piling up in 2026.
Take the case of Bonnie in Orlando, Florida, an elderly lady who’d spent her life working
as a puppeteer. No doubt her online profile showed how she often supported various causes. In 2026,
she received a phone call from her good friend Carl and learned that he’d landed himself in jail.
“It’s me, it’s Carl, I’m in jail,” he’d told her. “I was drinking and... I hit a pregnant lady, and
I broke my nose, and I’m—can you help me, please?” Bonnie later told the media that it sounded,
quote, “Absolutely exactly like him.” She didn’t even hesitate when
he asked for money for bail. Carl hung up and a few minutes later,
a man claiming to be Carl’s public defender called. He told Bonnie the bail was thousands
of dollars. They told her to put the cash in an envelope and gave her a fake case number
to write on the outside. A while later, someone
turned up at her house to collect the money. She was now out of a good chunk of her savings.
Bonnie was the ideal target: Single woman. Retired. Kind. In the scamming world: a sucker.
Her details could have been sold on the Dark Web and then the scammers who bought them
possibly found her social media profile and soon determined she had a friend named Carl.
All they needed now was to silent call Carl. With maybe just 3 seconds of audio,
less time than to take a sip of coffee, they could have re-created his voice.
When the scammers asked for a second round of money, Bonnie grew suspicious and called Carl.
He was sitting happily at home in the middle of having dinner.
Bonnie’s retirement “nest egg,” money she, quote, “desperately,” needed, was gone.
Bonnie’s case was at least fairly stress-free besides the financial loss.
Sometimes vishing is far more brutal. Another recent case saw a mother in California,
a veteran of the US Navy, received a call from men claiming to be a Mexican
drug cartel who’d kidnapped her daughter. They put the daughter on the line. She was
sobbing. As she sometimes did, she was having a panic attack. The scammers might have found her
issues with panic online. For the mom, everything was exactly like her daughter. They wanted
$20,000 or the daughter would get seriously hurt. Maybe they’d kill her. Maybe even traffic her.
The mother didn’t have $20,000. She and her husband’s entire life savings amounted to
$5,400 which they transferred to Mexico using MoneyGram and Western Union.
The ordeal lasted 5.5 hours. 5.5 hours of mental torture.
The fake kidnappers stayed on the phone with the mother almost throughout it all.
“I'm so sorry, Mom,” the daughter told her at one point, “I love you.”
The mom later said, “It was absolutely her voice.”
The scammers wanted even more money but when the parents said there was nothing to give,
the scammers told them they’d drop the daughter off in front of a Walmart in California.
Of course, when the parents turned up at the Walmart, there was no sign of her.
They immediately thought the worst. All this time, the parents had been
so incredibly stressed and been so involved on the phone that they’d
never thought to call their daughter’s phone. The FBI called it a “virtual kidnapping.”
The scammers had very likely used voice cloning software and may have looked at
a profile of the obviously very close family online. The sound of the sobbing had hijacked
the rational frontal cortex part of the parents’ brains. It left their limbic system’s fear and
stress mechanisms to guide their actions. Research states that in the US alone,
there are now approximately 2.56 billion scam calls per month. That represents
enough automated traffic to call every person in North America multiple times every 30 days.
It’s almost impossible to trace the numbers. Scammers rely on a vast network of internet-based
telephone providers, known as VoIP carriers, to route their calls around the world. Some of these
companies have been accused of knowingly allowing fraudulent calls through their networks, even when
the caller's identity has been disguised. The US Federal Communications Commission has taken
action against several such providers, including ordering telephone networks to block their calls.
But it’s evidently not enough. The system is broken. The safety
nets are gone. Which means the next time your phone rings it could be a trap.
And if you answer, you’re not just saying hello to a stranger.
You’re giving them permission to become you. It seems like there’s no way to beat the con
artists… but that isn’t true. Watch “Times Scammers Messed With the Wrong
People” to see what happens when they get a slice of karma. Or click on this.
